title: Candidozyma auris Colonization and Infection in Intensive Care Units: From Colonization to Candidemia and Clinical Outcomes—A Comprehensive Review
content: Background: Candidozyma auris (C. auris) is an emerging multidrug-resistant yeast that has become an important cause of healthcare-associated outbreaks, particularly in intensive care units (ICUs). Colonization frequently precedes invasive infection, yet the epidemiology, progression to candidemia, and mortality among critically ill patients remain incompletely characterized. Methods: We conducted a narrative review of published studies evaluating C. auris colonization and infection in ICU populations. Studies reporting colonization rates, progression to invasive infection, and mortality were synthesized. Pooled estimates were calculated using aggregated data from eligible observational studies. Results: Colonization rates varied widely according to local epidemiology, ranging from 0.2–0.4% in routine surveillance studies to over 50% during outbreaks. Across 17 observational studies including 1,879 colonized ICU patients, 616 developed invasive infection, yielding a pooled incidence of 32.8%, predominantly candidemia. The median interval from ICU admission to candidemia was 25.8 days. Among 13 studies including 1,354 colonized and/or infected ICU patients, the pooled 30-day in-hospital mortality was 36.4% (95% CI, 33.8–39.0%). In 12 studies comprising 396 patients with C. auris candidemia, pooled 30-day mortality was 45.9% (95% CI, 41.0–50.8%), significantly exceeding that in mixed colonized/infected populations. Conclusions: Candidozyma auris represents a major threat in ICUs because of its ability to establish persistent colonization, progress to invasive candidemia, and cause high mortality among critically ill patients. Early identification of colonized patients, rigorous infection prevention measures, and prompt antifungal management are essential to reduce transmission and improve clinical outcomes.
